opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we ran into very directly when we were building weather and climate models with neural operators. The most naive thing you can do is take the globe, unroll it onto a latitude-longitude grid, and treat it like an image, a rectangle. Then you apply a standard Fourier neural operator, which uses the FFT and implicitly assumes periodic boundaries in both directions.

The problem is that the Earth isn't a rectangle. Longitude wraps around nicely, so periodicity there is fine. Latitude doesn't. At the poles the whole top row of pixels collapses to a single point, so you have massive distortion and heavy oversampling near the poles. The model is also being told that the North Pole is adjacent to the South Pole, which is physically meaningless. Over a single step you might not notice. But in weather and climate you're doing autoregressive rollouts, feeding the model's predictions back in for hundreds or thousands of steps. Those small artifacts at the poles and boundaries accumulate, and you get blow-ups: energy builds up at high frequencies, you see spurious features, and the simulation eventually becomes unstable and diverges.

So what we did with the spherical Fourier neural operator was respect the geometry. Instead of the regular Fourier transform, we use spherical harmonics, the natural basis for functions on a sphere. Convolutions then become rotation-equivariant on the sphere, there's no artificial boundary, and the poles aren't special anymore. That one change made a dramatic difference. We could roll out stably for very long horizons, even out to a year of simulated time, and the energy spectrum stayed physically reasonable instead of drifting.

To me the broader lesson is that in scientific machine learning you can't just borrow architectures from computer vision and hope they work. The domain has structure: geometry, symmetries, conservation properties. If you build that into the model, you get stability and generalization almost for free. If you ignore it, you can get great short-term metrics while the model quietly falls apart over long time scales, which is exactly where science needs it to work.

r001.rationale: It says the rectangular latitude-longitude approach can accumulate artifacts and become unstable, while the spherical approach enabled stable rollouts over long horizons.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question that sits right at the heart of why neural operators matter for weather and climate, so let me unpack it.

If you think about the way most machine learning for weather started, it inherited the vision mindset. You take the globe, you unroll it onto a latitude-longitude grid, and now it looks like an image. A rectangle. And then you throw a convolutional network or a vision transformer at it, because that's what we had lying around. The problem is that the planet is not a rectangle. The moment you flatten a sphere, you introduce distortions. Near the equator a grid cell is roughly a square on the surface. Near the poles those same cells shrink to almost nothing in physical area, and the two vertical edges of your rectangle are actually the same longitude line, so the model has to learn that the left edge and the right edge are neighbors.

Why does that hurt stability? Because when you roll a forecast model forward autoregressively, six hours, then twelve, then days, every small inconsistency compounds. If the model treats the poles as a line of pixels rather than a point, you get artifacts there, spurious energy, little oscillations. If it doesn't perfectly respect periodicity in longitude, you get a seam. Those errors are tiny at step one and catastrophic at step a hundred. In FourCastNet's first version, which used adaptive Fourier neural operators on a flat grid, we saw exactly this kind of long-horizon blow-up. The forecasts were excellent for a week or so, and then the physics drifted into something unrealistic.

The sphere changes that picture. When we moved to spherical Fourier neural operators, the basis functions are spherical harmonics rather than planar Fourier modes. The geometry is built in. There is no pole singularity because the harmonics are smooth over the whole sphere, there is no seam because the representation is globally periodic by construction, and rotational symmetry is respected rather than approximated. What we found is that the same model, with the same training data, could run stably for a year of simulated time instead of a couple of weeks. It wasn't that the sphere made it more accurate on day three. It's that it stopped accumulating the kind of structured error that eventually makes a simulation go off the rails.

I think the deeper lesson is that stability in learned simulation is mostly about what inductive biases you bake in. Data alone will not teach a model that the Earth is round in a way that holds up under a thousand recursive steps. You can regularize, you can fine-tune on rollouts, and those help. But respecting the actual geometry of the domain is a much stronger lever. It's the difference between hoping the model learns the conservation structure and giving it an architecture where violating that structure is simply harder to express.

And this generalizes beyond weather. Any time you're learning a solution operator for a PDE, the choice of domain representation is really a choice about which symmetries you honor. Get that right and a lot of stability problems just dissolve.

r001.rationale: It says the flat-grid rectangular model eventually blows up, while the spherical representation lets the same model run stably for a year instead of a couple of weeks.

astra-6.text:
The geometry matters because it determines what your model has to learn. If you take a spherical world and represent it as a rectangle, you introduce artificial boundaries and distortions. Points that are close together on the sphere can look far apart on that map, and the distortion becomes particularly severe near the poles.

For a simulation, those aren’t just visual artifacts. They affect how information propagates, and small errors can accumulate as you roll the model forward. If you build the spherical geometry into the representation, you give the model the right notion of locality and continuity from the start.

That doesn’t automatically guarantee stability—you still need to consider the dynamics, conservation laws, and time stepping—but it removes a source of error. The model can spend its capacity learning the physics instead of compensating for the way we flattened the world.

r001.rationale: The response says spherical geometry removes a source of error and explains that errors can accumulate during rollout, but it never clearly states that a spherical representation produces a more stable rollout than a rectangular one.

sol-6.1.text:
The shape itself doesn’t guarantee stability, but choosing a representation that matches the geometry of the problem can make a big difference. For global weather, for example, we’re modeling dynamics on a sphere. If we flatten that into a rectangle, we introduce distortions and have to handle boundaries and the poles carefully. Those artifacts can become especially problematic when we repeatedly feed a model’s predictions back into itself.

Working directly on the sphere gives us a way to respect that geometry and avoid some of those artificial discontinuities. But we still need to capture the physics and control how errors accumulate over time. Geometry is an important part of stable simulation; it isn’t the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response says spherical modeling avoids some artificial discontinuities and that rectangular artifacts can be problematic over repeated predictions, but it never clearly states that a sphere produces a more stable simulation rollout than a rectangle.
